title: IAM Policies and Permissions
description: Understand IAM policy structure, identity-based vs resource-based policies, and permission evaluation logic.

data.text: An IAM policy is a JSON document that defines permissions. Policies describe who can access which resources and what actions they can perform. They are attached to IAM identities like users, groups, and roles, or to resources like S3 buckets.
Every policy has a Version field and a list of Statements. Each statement contains an Effect, an Action, and a Resource. You can also add a Condition for more fine-grained control.

rows: The language version. Use 2012-10-17 for new policies.
An array of individual permission statements.
An optional statement identifier for your own reference.
Allow or Deny. Determines whether the statement grants or blocks access.
The API actions allowed or denied (e.g., s3:ListBucket).
The ARN of the resource the action applies to.
Optional logic that restricts when the statement applies.

data.text: Identity-based policies are attached to IAM identities such as users, groups, and roles. Resource-based policies are attached directly to AWS resources, such as S3 bucket policies or Lambda resource policies.

data.title: Key Differences
items: Identity-based policies control what an identity can do. They are attached to users, groups, or roles.
Resource-based policies control who can access a specific resource. They are attached to resources like S3 buckets.
Both types work together. For an action to be allowed, both the identity-based policy and the resource-based policy must allow it.

data.text: A permissions boundary is an advanced feature that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant. It acts as a guardrail: even if an administrator attaches a broad policy, the boundary can limit the actual permissions.

When a request is made, AWS evaluates all applicable policies by default. The evaluation follows these rules: by default, everything is denied. An explicit Allow in any applicable policy overrides the default. An explicit Deny in any policy overrides any Allow.

terms.definition: A policy attached to an IAM identity that defines what that identity can do.
A policy attached directly to an AWS resource that defines who can access it.
A guardrail that sets the maximum permissions an identity can have, regardless of attached policies.
A direct Deny statement in any applicable policy that overrides all Allows.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Policies are JSON documents with statements that allow or deny actions on resources
Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, or roles
Resource-based policies attach directly to AWS resources
Permissions boundaries limit the maximum permissions an identity can receive
AWS evaluates all policies together; explicit Deny overrides Allow
